I was fifteen the spring I refereed my first under-ten soccer game, and I had spent the week memorizing the rulebook the league mailed me. I knew the dimensions of the penalty area to the inch. What the rulebook had failed to mention was the sideline.

The game was the Hornets against the Rockets on Field Four behind the middle school. Within five minutes a father in a red cap was shouting my name, which he had read off the clipboard, and following it with suggestions. By halftime three more parents had joined him. They stood with their coffee at the very edge of the touchline, close enough that I could hear the ice rattle in one of their cups, and they announced every call before I made it.

The players, meanwhile, were having a wonderful time. A small girl on the Rockets ran the length of the field twice, laughing, without ever touching the ball. A Hornets defender stopped to tie his shoe in the middle of an attack. Nobody on the field was keeping score except the parents, who were keeping it loudly.

With four minutes left and the score tied, a Hornets forward kicked the ball past the Rockets' goalkeeper while standing well past the last defender. I blew the whistle and raised my arm for offside. The man in the red cap walked onto the field. He told me I had cost his son a goal, and that a referee who could not see the play from twenty feet away should find another hobby.

I remember the heat in my face more than anything he said. Then the Hornets coach, a soft-spoken woman I had barely noticed, crossed the field, put a hand on the man's shoulder, and asked him to wait in the parking lot until the game was over. He went. She turned to me, said that the call was right, and told me to restart play.

The game ended in a tie. Afterward, the forward who had been offside came over and asked me what offside meant. I explained it with two water bottles and a pine cone on the grass, and he listened with great seriousness and then ran off to find his juice box.

I refereed for four more seasons. I learned to stand where I could see the play and to let the sideline say what it liked. But I never stopped thinking that the adults at those games had come to watch a different contest from the one their children were playing.

At seven-forty, Mrs. Avila
steps off the curb on Halsted Street
in her orange vest and her husband's old gloves
and lifts the red sign like a lantern.

The trucks stop. The buses stop.
A man in a silver car
who has somewhere he would rather be
stops, and drums on the wheel, and waits.

Some mornings a parent waves from a car,
and she lifts one glove without turning,
her eyes still on the children.

Then the children cross in their loose
and wandering lines, backpacks bobbing,
a boy reading as he walks,
two sisters arguing about a sandwich,
and she counts them under her breath,
every morning, every one,
the way my grandmother counted stitches,
as if the whole thing might unravel otherwise.

In thirty years, they say, she has missed
four days, one for each grandchild.
She knows which ones dawdle
and which ones run for the last bell,
and she calls them by their names,
which none of them remember telling her.

On snow days she is out there early,
salting the curb from a coffee can,
and on the last day of school
the children tape their drawings to the light pole.

When the last small coat is safely over,
she lowers the sign, and the street
starts up again behind her,
impatient, enormous, roaring,
and she walks back to the corner
to wait for the next one.

For most of my childhood, the shoe repair shop on Cort Street smelled of leather, glue, and the peppermints Mr. Halloran kept in a jar beside the register. I went there with my mother every fall, when the heels on my school shoes had worn down at an angle, and I would sit on the bench by the window and watch him work while she ran her errands.

He worked at a long bench under a hanging lamp, with his tools arranged on a strip of felt in an order that never changed. He could take a heel off a shoe in less time than it took me to unwrap a peppermint, and while he worked he told me about the shoes that came through his door: a bride's satin slippers, a mail carrier's boots that had walked, he estimated, twelve thousand miles, a pair of tap shoes he had repaired for the same dancer for forty years.

I asked him once how he knew where a shoe needed fixing. He held up one of mine and turned it slowly in the light. Every shoe, he said, tells you how its owner walks. Mine told him that I leaned to the left and dragged my right foot when I was tired, both of which turned out to be true.

When I was in high school, the shop's hours grew shorter. People were buying cheaper shoes, Mr. Halloran told my mother, shoes that were cheaper to throw away than to fix. The jar of peppermints was sometimes empty. One spring the windows were papered over, and a sign appeared announcing that the building would become a phone store. I remember walking past the papered windows and feeling that something had been taken from the street without anyone asking.

I was away at college when he died. My mother sent me the notice from the newspaper, and folded inside it was a small brown envelope she had found when she cleaned out a closet. It held a heel tip from one of my childhood shoes, worn down at a sharp angle on one side, with my name written on the envelope in his careful printing. She thought I had brought it home from the shop as a souvenir. I have no memory of doing so.

I keep the envelope in my desk. Some evenings I take out the heel tip and turn it over in my hand the way he turned my shoe in the light, and I think about all the people who walked into that shop and out again a little more evenly, and about how few of them will remember the man at the long bench.

When I was eleven, my family spent two weeks every August at my uncle's cabin on a lake, a place with spotty electricity, no television and one shelf of water-damaged board games. For the first three days of every visit I was miserable. I followed my mother around asking what there was to do, and she gave the same answer every year: "Figure it out."

By the fourth day, I usually had. One summer I built a dam across the creek behind the cabin and spent a week adjusting it, stone by stone, until the pool behind it was deep enough to float a leaf boat. Another summer I taught myself to whittle with a dull pocketknife and produced a spoon, a whistle and a long, lumpy object I insisted was a fish. None of these projects were planned. Each of them began in the dull, empty stretch of an afternoon when there was simply time to fill.

Children today rarely meet that stretch. A spare ten minutes in a waiting room or the back seat of a car can be filled instantly with a game or a video, and most of us, adults included, fill it. I understand why. Boredom is uncomfortable, and a screen ends the discomfort in seconds.

But psychologists who study boredom have suggested that the discomfort may be the point. In one frequently described kind of experiment, people who first complete a dull task, such as copying numbers from a phone book, then come up with more uses for an ordinary object than people who skip the dull task. The researchers' explanation is that boredom pushes the mind to go looking for something to do, and that the search itself is where new ideas begin.

I am not arguing that children should be denied their games, or that every long car ride must be endured in silence. I am suggesting that we stop treating boredom as an emergency. An afternoon with time to fill is an invitation, and children can only learn to accept it if they are occasionally left alone long enough to hear it.

My uncle sold the cabin years ago. I still have the lumpy fish. It sits on the windowsill above my desk, and when I find myself reaching for my phone in an idle moment, I sometimes look at it instead and wait to see what my mind will come up with on its own.

It is one of the most repeated facts in the world, printed on posters, quoted in classrooms and offered as an excuse for small fishbowls: a goldfish has a memory of three seconds. Every lap of its bowl, the story goes, is a brand-new adventure.

In study after study, trained goldfish have responded to the signal weeks later, and in some cases months later.

Goldfish can also learn more complicated tasks. They have been trained to push a lever for food, to swim through a simple maze, and even to tell two pieces of music apart. Fish trained to feed during one particular hour of the day will gather at the feeding spot shortly before that hour, as if keeping time.

Why, then, does the three-second figure survive? Part of the answer may be that it is convenient. A creature that forgets everything has little need for space, variety or company, and a person who has just bought a goldfish in a small glass bowl may find that a comforting thought. Myths that excuse our habits tend to be the ones we are slowest to give up.

None of this means a goldfish thinks the way a dog or a person does. Its brain is small and organized very differently from ours.
